start.README.md:
# stoke: an incremental build engine for text artifacts

`stoke` keeps a small in-memory store of text files, a set of build rules that derive some files from others, and it rebuilds only what is out of date. It is driven by a script on standard input and reports every step on standard output, so that its behaviour can be checked exactly. Nothing is read from or written to the real file system.

Build and run it as `build/stoke`, built with `go build -o build/stoke .` (package `main` in the module root; `go.mod` is provided, standard library only). The program reads the whole of standard input, runs the script line by line and exits.

## 1. Script and output

* A script is a sequence of lines. Leading and trailing white space of a line is ignored; empty lines and lines starting with `#` do nothing.
* The first word of a line is the command; words are separated by single or multiple spaces. Command names are lower-case and case-sensitive.
* Every command prints zero or more lines to standard output (given below). A failing command prints one `error: ...` line and the script continues with the next line.
* Exit status: `1` if at least one line starting with `error:` or `fail ` was printed during the run, otherwise `0`. Nothing is ever printed to standard error that matters.
* The commands are: `put`, `rule`, `build`, `show`, `digest`, `ls`, `stats`, `status`, `clean`. Any other first word prints `error: unknown command 'WORD'`.

## 2. Paths, files and text

A path is made of letters, digits and the characters `_ . / -`. It is split at `/` into segments and no segment may be empty, `.` or `..` (so a path does not start or end with `/` and has no `//`). In rule targets and rule dependencies a path may also contain one `%` (see section 4). Anything else is a bad path: `error: bad path 'PATH'`.

The store maps paths to *files*. A file is a text (a string of ASCII characters; it may contain newlines and tabs) plus bookkeeping described below. A file is either a **source** (created by `put`) or **derived** (produced by a rule). A path is *derived* if a rule matches it (section 4), whether or not the file exists yet; every other path is a source path.

The *digest* of a text is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its UTF-8 bytes, written as eight lower-case hex digits: start with `h = 0x811c9dc5`; for each byte `b`, `h = h XOR b`, then `h = (h * 0x01000193) mod 2^32`. The digest of the empty text is `811c9dc5`.

The store has a **logical clock**, an integer that starts at 0. It is advanced by one (a *tick*) every time a file is written by `put` or by an action, and by `touch` (there is no `touch` in this build); each file remembers the clock value of its last write as its *stamp*.

## 3. Commands that change or inspect files

* `put PATH [TEXT]` creates or replaces a source file. `TEXT` is everything after the single space that follows `PATH` (it may contain further spaces; white space at the end of the line is not part of it; it may be absent, giving an empty text). In `TEXT`, the escapes `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab) and `\\` (one backslash) are decoded; a backslash followed by any other character stays as it is. The file gets a new stamp (one tick). Prints `wrote PATH (N bytes)` where `N` is the length of the decoded text in bytes. Errors: no path -> `error: usage: put PATH [TEXT]`; a bad path; a derived path -> `error: 'PATH' is derived, not a source file`.
* `show PATH` prints `PATH = "TEXT"` with the text encoded the opposite way (a backslash becomes `\\`, a newline `\n`, a tab `\t`). Unknown file: `error: no such file 'PATH'`. Wrong word count: `error: usage: show PATH`.
* `digest PATH` prints `PATH DIGEST`. Same errors as `show` (usage text `usage: digest PATH`).
* `ls` prints one line `PATH DIGEST KIND` for every file in the store, sorted by path (plain byte order), where `KIND` is `derived` if the path is derived, else `source`. Arguments are ignored.
* `stats` prints `files=F rules=R actions=A clock=C`: the number of files, the number of rules, the number of action executions so far (failed attempts included; skipped ones not) and the clock. Arguments are ignored.
* `clean [PATH...]` deletes derived files. Without arguments it deletes every existing derived file; with arguments it deletes exactly those files. If an argument is not the path of an existing derived file the command prints `error: 'PATH' is not a derived file` for the first such argument (in the order given) and deletes nothing. Prints `cleaned N files` (`N` counts distinct deleted files; also for `0` and `1`). Deleting a file also forgets how it was built.

## 4. Rules

`rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` declares how `TARGET` is made. `<-` and `:` are words of their own. There may be no dependencies. `:!` is not a separator in this build. Arguments are the words after the action name.

Checks, in this order, each with its error (`error: ` is implied):

1. `rule syntax: rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` if the second word is not `<-`, there is no separator word, or no action name follows it.
2. `bad path 'P'` for the first of target, dependencies (left to right) that is not a valid path.
3. `stem in dependency without stem in target` if a dependency contains `%` but the target does not.
4. `unknown action 'NAME'`, or `bad arguments for 'NAME'` (section 5).
5. `duplicate rule for 'TARGET'` if an earlier rule has exactly the same target text.
6. `'FILE' already exists as a source file` if a file already in the store would be made by the new rule (for a pattern rule: the first such file in byte order); rules never take over existing files.

On success it prints `rule TARGET`.

**Pattern rules.** A target with a `%` is a pattern. `%` stands for a non-empty *stem* (it may contain `/`): the pattern `out/%.up` matches `out/a/b.up` with stem `a/b`, but not `out/.up`. In the dependencies of a pattern rule every `%` is replaced by the stem. Several dependencies may each contain a `%`; dependencies without one are fixed.

**Which rule makes a path.** An exact rule (target without `%`) whose target equals the path wins. Otherwise, among the pattern rules that match the path, the one with the most literal characters (target length minus one) wins; on a tie the earlier declared rule wins. If no rule matches, the path is a source path.

## 5. Actions

Every action computes the text of the target from the texts of the dependencies, taken in the order written. Let `IN` be those texts joined with a single `\n` between them (`IN` is empty when there are no dependencies); *lines of X* means X split at `\n`, dropping one empty last piece (so the empty text has no lines and `a\n` has one). Actions work on ASCII only.

| action | result |
|---|---|
| `cat` | `IN`. |
| `lower` | `IN` with `A`-`Z` turned into `a`-`z`. |
| `rev` | `IN` with its characters in reverse order. |
| `count` | the length of `IN` in characters, in decimal. |
| `head N` | the first `N` lines of `IN` joined with `\n` (all of them if there are fewer). `N` is 1 to 9 decimal digits. |
| `uniq` | the lines of `IN` with each run of identical consecutive lines reduced to one, joined with `\n`. |
| `grep WORD` | the lines of `IN` that contain `WORD` as a substring, joined with `\n` (exactly one argument). |
| `tag NAME` | `<NAME>` followed by `IN` followed by `</NAME>`; `NAME` is one argument: a letter followed by letters and digits. |
| `sum` | the sum of all white-space separated words of `IN` that look like an integer (an optional `-` and 1 to 9 digits), in decimal; other words are ignored. |
| `const [TEXT...]` | the arguments joined with single spaces (empty if none); the dependencies are not looked at. |
| `failif WORD` | `IN`, unless `IN` contains `WORD` as a substring: then the action *fails* with the message `found WORD` (exactly one argument). |
| `fail` | nothing: the action always *fails* with the message `always fails`. |

These are the only actions of this build; any other name is an unknown action. An action with arguments of the wrong number or shape is `bad arguments`. Actions without arguments listed above take none.

## 6. Building

`build [OPTION...] TARGET...` brings the targets up to date, in the order given. Options come first (words that start with `-` before the first target): `--keep-going` (or `-k`). Every word after the first word that does not start with `-` is a target, whatever it looks like. Validation happens before any work and stops the command at the first problem, in this order: an unknown option (`error: unknown option 'WORD'`); no targets (`error: build needs at least one target`); the first target that is not a valid path without `%` (`error: bad path 'P'`).

Bringing a path up to date (*visiting* it) works like this. Each path is visited at most once per command; a second request for it gets the same outcome and prints nothing. The outcome is one of *source*, *fresh*, *built*, *failed*, *blocked*.

1. Find the rule for the path. If there is none: when the file exists the outcome is *source* (nothing is printed); otherwise print `error: no rule to make 'PATH'`, followed by ` (needed by 'REQUESTER')` when the path was visited as a dependency of another path, and the outcome is *failed*.
2. If the path is already being visited further up (a cycle), print `error: cycle A -> B -> ... -> A` where the list starts at the first occurrence of the path on the chain of paths being visited and ends with the path again. The outcome is *failed*.
3. Visit the dependencies (stems filled in) from left to right, so everything a path needs is reported before the path itself. If any dependency is *failed* or *blocked*, print `blocked PATH`; the outcome is *blocked*.
4. Decide whether the path is **stale**. The *key* of a rule application is the digest of the text `ACTION` + `\x1f` (the byte 0x1f) + the digests of the dependency texts joined with `,`, where `ACTION` is the action name and its arguments joined with single spaces. Every derived file remembers the key of the application that made it. The path is stale if its file does not exist, or its remembered key differs from the current key (because a dependency's text changed, so that its digest changed). This gives **early cutoff**: when a dependency is rebuilt to exactly the same text, nothing that depends on it is rebuilt. Stamps play no role in this build.
5. If the path is not stale, print `skip PATH`; the outcome is *fresh*.
6. Otherwise run the action (it counts in `stats` even if it fails). If it fails, print `fail PATH: MESSAGE`; the outcome is *failed*, and the file (if any) is left as it was.
7. If it succeeds, the file gets the new text and a new stamp (one tick) and the new key and the line is `same PATH` if the file already existed with exactly this text, else `run PATH`. The outcome is *built*.

Failure policy. Without `--keep-going` the command stops at the first failure (any line `fail ...`, `error: no rule ...` or `error: cycle ...` of this command): after that line nothing more is visited or printed except the final summary line. With `--keep-going` the command carries on: the other dependencies and the other targets are still visited, and only the paths that depend on a failure are *blocked*.

At the end of every `build` command that got past validation (also when it stopped early) it prints `summary: ran=R same=S skipped=K failed=F blocked=B`: the number of paths with the lines `run`, `same`, `skip`, `fail`/`error: no rule`/`error: cycle` (each such line counts one *failed*, also the one that stopped the command) and `blocked`. Sources and halting add nothing.

## 7. Status

`status TARGET...` (validation as for building; no targets: `error: status needs at least one target`) reports what a build would find, without running anything and without changing any file. It visits paths like a build does (once each, dependencies first, left to right; sources print nothing; `error: no rule to make ...` and `error: cycle ...` are printed in the same way), and prints for every derived path one line, in visiting order:

* nothing at all if one of its dependencies had an error (the path itself then counts as erroneous too);
* otherwise `stale PATH (REASON)` with the first applicable reason: `missing` (no file), `dep D` (`D` is the first dependency, left to right, that was reported stale), `changed` (the remembered key differs from the key computed from the current texts of the dependencies);
* otherwise `fresh PATH`.

Note that `status` is conservative: a path below a stale path is reported stale even though a build might cut off at the stale path.

## Examples

prompt: We keep regenerating text artifacts by hand and I'd like a proper little build engine for it. The tool is called `stoke` and the whole behaviour is written down in `README.md` in this repository. Please implement it in Go; the program must be `build/stoke`, built with `go build -o build/stoke .` (package `main` in the module root; `go.mod` is provided, standard library only). `python3 tests/run_examples.py` runs the visible examples; the real checks are far more thorough, so read the README closely, especially the part about how staleness is decided (content digests and early cutoff), the order of the trace lines and failures and what gets blocked.

solution.src/hashing.py:
"""Content digests: FNV-1a (32 bit) over the UTF-8 bytes, shown as eight lower-case hex digits."""


def digest(text: str) -> str:
    h = 0x811C9DC5
    for b in text.encode("utf-8"):
        h ^= b
        h = (h * 0x01000193) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return "%08x" % h

start.README.md:
# kiln: an incremental build engine for text artifacts

`kiln` keeps a small in-memory store of text files, a set of build rules that derive some files from others, and it rebuilds only what is out of date. It is driven by a script on standard input and reports every step on standard output, so that its behaviour can be checked exactly. Nothing is read from or written to the real file system.

Build and run it as `python3 src/kiln.py` (entry point `src/kiln.py`; other modules go next to it in `src/`). The program reads the whole of standard input, runs the script line by line and exits.

## 1. Script and output

* A script is a sequence of lines. Leading and trailing white space of a line is ignored; empty lines and lines starting with `#` do nothing.
* The first word of a line is the command; words are separated by single or multiple spaces. Command names are lower-case and case-sensitive.
* Every command prints zero or more lines to standard output (given below). A failing command prints one `error: ...` line and the script continues with the next line.
* Exit status: `1` if at least one line starting with `error:` or `fail ` was printed during the run, otherwise `0`. Nothing is ever printed to standard error that matters.
* The commands are: `write`, `rule`, `make`, `show`, `digest`, `ls`, `stats`, `status`, `clean`, `touch`. Any other first word prints `error: unknown command 'WORD'`.

## 2. Paths, files and text

A path is made of letters, digits and the characters `_ . / -`. It is split at `/` into segments and no segment may be empty, `.` or `..` (so a path does not start or end with `/` and has no `//`). A `%` is not allowed in any path. Anything else is a bad path: `error: bad path 'PATH'`.

The store maps paths to *files*. A file is a text (a string of ASCII characters; it may contain newlines and tabs) plus bookkeeping described below. A file is either a **source** (created by `write`) or **derived** (produced by a rule). A path is *derived* if a rule matches it (section 4), whether or not the file exists yet; every other path is a source path.

The *digest* of a text is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its UTF-8 bytes, written as eight lower-case hex digits: start with `h = 0x811c9dc5`; for each byte `b`, `h = h XOR b`, then `h = (h * 0x01000193) mod 2^32`. The digest of the empty text is `811c9dc5`.

The store has a **logical clock**, an integer that starts at 0. It is advanced by one (a *tick*) every time a file is written by `write` or by an action, and by `touch`; each file remembers the clock value of its last write as its *stamp*.

## 3. Commands that change or inspect files

* `write PATH [TEXT]` creates or replaces a source file. `TEXT` is everything after the single space that follows `PATH` (it may contain further spaces; white space at the end of the line is not part of it; it may be absent, giving an empty text). In `TEXT`, the escapes `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab) and `\\` (one backslash) are decoded; a backslash followed by any other character stays as it is. The file gets a new stamp (one tick). Prints `wrote PATH (N bytes)` where `N` is the length of the decoded text in bytes. Errors: no path -> `error: usage: write PATH [TEXT]`; a bad path; a derived path -> `error: 'PATH' is derived, not a source file`.
* `show PATH` prints `PATH = "TEXT"` with the text encoded the opposite way (a backslash becomes `\\`, a newline `\n`, a tab `\t`). Unknown file: `error: no such file 'PATH'`. Wrong word count: `error: usage: show PATH`.
* `digest PATH` prints `PATH DIGEST`. Same errors as `show` (usage text `usage: digest PATH`).
* `ls` prints one line `PATH DIGEST KIND` for every file in the store, sorted by path (plain byte order), where `KIND` is `derived` if the path is derived, else `source`. Arguments are ignored.
* `stats` prints `files=F rules=R actions=A clock=C`: the number of files, the number of rules, the number of action executions so far (failed attempts included; skipped ones not) and the clock. Arguments are ignored.
* `touch PATH` gives an existing file a new stamp (one tick) without changing its text and prints `touched PATH`. Errors: `error: usage: touch PATH`, `error: no such file 'PATH'`.
* `clean [PATH...]` deletes derived files. Without arguments it deletes every existing derived file; with arguments it deletes exactly those files. If an argument is not the path of an existing derived file the command prints `error: 'PATH' is not a derived file` for the first such argument (in the order given) and deletes nothing. Prints `cleaned N files` (`N` counts distinct deleted files; also for `0` and `1`). Deleting a file also forgets how it was built.

## 4. Rules

`rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` declares how `TARGET` is made. `<-` and `:` are words of their own. There may be no dependencies. `:!` is not a separator in this build. Arguments are the words after the action name.

Checks, in this order, each with its error (`error: ` is implied):

1. `rule syntax: rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` if the second word is not `<-`, there is no separator word, or no action name follows it.
2. `bad path 'P'` for the first of target, dependencies (left to right) that is not a valid path.
4. `unknown action 'NAME'`, or `bad arguments for 'NAME'` (section 5).
5. `duplicate rule for 'TARGET'` if an earlier rule has exactly the same target text.
6. `'FILE' already exists as a source file` if a file already in the store would be made by the new rule (for a pattern rule: the first such file in byte order); rules never take over existing files.

On success it prints `rule TARGET`.

**Which rule makes a path.** An exact rule (target without `%`) whose target equals the path wins. If no rule matches, the path is a source path.

## 5. Actions

Every action computes the text of the target from the texts of the dependencies, taken in the order written. Let `IN` be those texts joined with a single `\n` between them (`IN` is empty when there are no dependencies); *lines of X* means X split at `\n`, dropping one empty last piece (so the empty text has no lines and `a\n` has one). Actions work on ASCII only.

| action | result |
|---|---|
| `cat` | `IN`. |
| `lower` | `IN` with `A`-`Z` turned into `a`-`z`. |
| `rev` | `IN` with its characters in reverse order. |
| `count` | the length of `IN` in characters, in decimal. |
| `head N` | the first `N` lines of `IN` joined with `\n` (all of them if there are fewer). `N` is 1 to 9 decimal digits. |
| `uniq` | the lines of `IN` with each run of identical consecutive lines reduced to one, joined with `\n`. |
| `grep WORD` | the lines of `IN` that contain `WORD` as a substring, joined with `\n` (exactly one argument). |
| `sum` | the sum of all white-space separated words of `IN` that look like an integer (an optional `-` and 1 to 9 digits), in decimal; other words are ignored. |
| `cap N` | like `sum`, but at most `N` (1 to 9 decimal digits). |
| `const [TEXT...]` | the arguments joined with single spaces (empty if none); the dependencies are not looked at. |
| `failif WORD` | `IN`, unless `IN` contains `WORD` as a substring: then the action *fails* with the message `found WORD` (exactly one argument). |
| `fail` | nothing: the action always *fails* with the message `always fails`. |

These are the only actions of this build; any other name is an unknown action. An action with arguments of the wrong number or shape is `bad arguments`. Actions without arguments listed above take none.

## 6. Building

`make [OPTION...] TARGET...` brings the targets up to date, in the order given. Options come first (words that start with `-` before the first target): `--max N`. Every word after the first word that does not start with `-` is a target, whatever it looks like. Validation happens before any work and stops the command at the first problem, in this order: an unknown option (`error: unknown option 'WORD'`); a `--max` without a decimal number after it (`error: bad --max value 'X'`, with `X` empty if the word is missing); no targets (`error: make needs at least one target`); the first target that is not a valid path without `%` (`error: bad path 'P'`).

Bringing a path up to date (*visiting* it) works like this. Each path is visited at most once per command; a second request for it gets the same outcome and prints nothing. The outcome is one of *source*, *fresh*, *built*, *failed*, *blocked*.

1. Find the rule for the path. If there is none: when the file exists the outcome is *source* (nothing is printed); otherwise print `error: no rule to make 'PATH'`, followed by ` (needed by 'REQUESTER')` when the path was visited as a dependency of another path, and the outcome is *failed*.
2. If the path is already being visited further up (a cycle), print `error: cycle A -> B -> ... -> A` where the list starts at the first occurrence of the path on the chain of paths being visited and ends with the path again. The outcome is *failed*.
3. Visit the dependencies (stems filled in) from left to right, so everything a path needs is reported before the path itself. If any dependency is *failed* or *blocked*, print `blocked PATH`; the outcome is *blocked*.
4. Decide whether the path is **stale**. It is stale if its file does not exist, or if any dependency has a stamp greater than the stamp of its file. Texts and digests play no role: a dependency that was rebuilt (or touched) makes everything above it stale even when its text came out identical, because every write ticks the clock. There is no early cutoff.
5. If the path is not stale, print `skip PATH`; the outcome is *fresh*.
6. Otherwise the action has to run. If the command has a budget (`--max N`) and `N` actions have already been executed by this command, print `halt: budget of N actions reached` and *stop the whole command* (nothing else is visited). `--max 0` therefore halts at the first action that has to run.
7. Run the action (this counts against the budget even if it fails; it also counts in `stats`). If it fails, print `fail PATH: MESSAGE`; the outcome is *failed*, and the file (if any) is left as it was.
8. If it succeeds, the file gets the new text and a new stamp (one tick) and the line is `same PATH` if the file already existed with exactly this text, else `run PATH`. The outcome is *built*.

Failure policy. The command stops at the first failure (any line `fail ...`, `error: no rule ...` or `error: cycle ...` of this command): after that line nothing more is visited or printed except the final summary line.

At the end of every `make` command that got past validation (also when it stopped early) it prints `result: ran=R same=S skipped=K failed=F blocked=B`: the number of paths with the lines `run`, `same`, `skip`, `fail`/`error: no rule`/`error: cycle` (each such line counts one *failed*, also the one that stopped the command) and `blocked`. Sources and halting add nothing.

## 7. Status

`status TARGET...` (validation as for building; no targets: `error: status needs at least one target`) reports what a build would find, without running anything and without changing any file. It visits paths like a build does (once each, dependencies first, left to right; sources print nothing; `error: no rule to make ...` and `error: cycle ...` are printed in the same way), and prints for every derived path one line, in visiting order:

* nothing at all if one of its dependencies had an error (the path itself then counts as erroneous too);
* otherwise `stale PATH (REASON)` with the first applicable reason: `missing` (no file), `dep D` (`D` is the first dependency, left to right, that was reported stale), `changed` (some dependency has a greater stamp);
* otherwise `fresh PATH`.

Note that a stale dependency makes every path above it stale in the report.

## Examples

start.README.md:
# anvil: an incremental build engine for text artifacts

`anvil` keeps a small in-memory store of text files, a set of build rules that derive some files from others, and it rebuilds only what is out of date. It is driven by a script on standard input and reports every step on standard output, so that its behaviour can be checked exactly. Nothing is read from or written to the real file system.

Build and run it as `build/anvil`, built with `go build -o build/anvil .` (package `main` in the module root; `go.mod` is provided, standard library only). The program reads the whole of standard input, runs the script line by line and exits.

## 1. Script and output

* A script is a sequence of lines. Leading and trailing white space of a line is ignored; empty lines and lines starting with `#` do nothing.
* The first word of a line is the command; words are separated by single or multiple spaces. Command names are lower-case and case-sensitive.
* Every command prints zero or more lines to standard output (given below). A failing command prints one `error: ...` line and the script continues with the next line.
* Exit status: `1` if at least one line starting with `error:` or `fail ` was printed during the run, otherwise `0`. Nothing is ever printed to standard error that matters.
* The commands are: `set`, `rule`, `want`, `show`, `digest`, `ls`, `stats`, `status`, `clean`, `touch`. Any other first word prints `error: unknown command 'WORD'`.

## 2. Paths, files and text

A path is made of letters, digits and the characters `_ . / -`. It is split at `/` into segments and no segment may be empty, `.` or `..` (so a path does not start or end with `/` and has no `//`). In rule targets and rule dependencies a path may also contain one `%` (see section 4). Anything else is a bad path: `error: bad path 'PATH'`.

The store maps paths to *files*. A file is a text (a string of ASCII characters; it may contain newlines and tabs) plus bookkeeping described below. A file is either a **source** (created by `set`) or **derived** (produced by a rule). A path is *derived* if a rule matches it (section 4), whether or not the file exists yet; every other path is a source path.

The *digest* of a text is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its UTF-8 bytes, written as eight lower-case hex digits: start with `h = 0x811c9dc5`; for each byte `b`, `h = h XOR b`, then `h = (h * 0x01000193) mod 2^32`. The digest of the empty text is `811c9dc5`.

The store has a **logical clock**, an integer that starts at 0. It is advanced by one (a *tick*) every time a file is written by `set` or by an action, and by `touch`; each file remembers the clock value of its last write as its *stamp*.

## 3. Commands that change or inspect files

* `set PATH [TEXT]` creates or replaces a source file. `TEXT` is everything after the single space that follows `PATH` (it may contain further spaces; white space at the end of the line is not part of it; it may be absent, giving an empty text). In `TEXT`, the escapes `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab) and `\\` (one backslash) are decoded; a backslash followed by any other character stays as it is. The file gets a new stamp (one tick). Prints `wrote PATH (N bytes)` where `N` is the length of the decoded text in bytes. Errors: no path -> `error: usage: set PATH [TEXT]`; a bad path; a derived path -> `error: 'PATH' is derived, not a source file`.
* `show PATH` prints `PATH = "TEXT"` with the text encoded the opposite way (a backslash becomes `\\`, a newline `\n`, a tab `\t`). Unknown file: `error: no such file 'PATH'`. Wrong word count: `error: usage: show PATH`.
* `digest PATH` prints `PATH DIGEST`. Same errors as `show` (usage text `usage: digest PATH`).
* `ls` prints one line `PATH DIGEST KIND` for every file in the store, sorted by path (plain byte order), where `KIND` is `derived` if the path is derived, else `source`. Arguments are ignored.
* `stats` prints `files=F rules=R actions=A clock=C`: the number of files, the number of rules, the number of action executions so far (failed attempts included; skipped ones not) and the clock. Arguments are ignored.
* `touch PATH` gives an existing file a new stamp (one tick) without changing its text and prints `touched PATH`. Errors: `error: usage: touch PATH`, `error: no such file 'PATH'`.
* `clean [PATH...]` deletes derived files. Without arguments it deletes every existing derived file; with arguments it deletes exactly those files. If an argument is not the path of an existing derived file the command prints `error: 'PATH' is not a derived file` for the first such argument (in the order given) and deletes nothing. Prints `cleaned N files` (`N` counts distinct deleted files; also for `0` and `1`). Deleting a file also forgets how it was built.

## 4. Rules

`rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` declares how `TARGET` is made. `<-` and `:` are words of their own. There may be no dependencies. A rule written with `:!` instead of `:` is an **always-rule** (see section 6). Arguments are the words after the action name.

Checks, in this order, each with its error (`error: ` is implied):

1. `rule syntax: rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` if the second word is not `<-`, there is no separator word, or no action name follows it.
2. `bad path 'P'` for the first of target, dependencies (left to right) that is not a valid path.
3. `stem in dependency without stem in target` if a dependency contains `%` but the target does not.
4. `unknown action 'NAME'`, or `bad arguments for 'NAME'` (section 5).
5. `duplicate rule for 'TARGET'` if an earlier rule has exactly the same target text.
6. `'FILE' already exists as a source file` if a file already in the store would be made by the new rule (for a pattern rule: the first such file in byte order); rules never take over existing files.

On success it prints `rule TARGET`.

**Pattern rules.** A target with a `%` is a pattern. `%` stands for a non-empty *stem* (it may contain `/`): the pattern `out/%.up` matches `out/a/b.up` with stem `a/b`, but not `out/.up`. In the dependencies of a pattern rule every `%` is replaced by the stem. Several dependencies may each contain a `%`; dependencies without one are fixed.

**Which rule makes a path.** An exact rule (target without `%`) whose target equals the path wins. Otherwise, among the pattern rules that match the path, the one with the most literal characters (target length minus one) wins; on a tie the earlier declared rule wins. If no rule matches, the path is a source path.

## 5. Actions

Every action computes the text of the target from the texts of the dependencies, taken in the order written. Let `IN` be those texts joined with a single `\n` between them (`IN` is empty when there are no dependencies); *lines of X* means X split at `\n`, dropping one empty last piece (so the empty text has no lines and `a\n` has one). Actions work on ASCII only.

| action | result |
|---|---|
| `cat` | `IN`. |
| `lower` | `IN` with `A`-`Z` turned into `a`-`z`. |
| `count` | the length of `IN` in characters, in decimal. |
| `lines` | the number of lines of `IN`, in decimal. |
| `head N` | the first `N` lines of `IN` joined with `\n` (all of them if there are fewer). `N` is 1 to 9 decimal digits. |
| `uniq` | the lines of `IN` with each run of identical consecutive lines reduced to one, joined with `\n`. |
| `tag NAME` | `<NAME>` followed by `IN` followed by `</NAME>`; `NAME` is one argument: a letter followed by letters and digits. |
| `sum` | the sum of all white-space separated words of `IN` that look like an integer (an optional `-` and 1 to 9 digits), in decimal; other words are ignored. |
| `cap N` | like `sum`, but at most `N` (1 to 9 decimal digits). |
| `const [TEXT...]` | the arguments joined with single spaces (empty if none); the dependencies are not looked at. |
| `fail` | nothing: the action always *fails* with the message `always fails`. |

These are the only actions of this build; any other name is an unknown action. An action with arguments of the wrong number or shape is `bad arguments`. Actions without arguments listed above take none.

## 6. Building

`want [OPTION...] TARGET...` brings the targets up to date, in the order given. Options come first (words that start with `-` before the first target): `--keep-going` (or `-k`) and `--max N`. Every word after the first word that does not start with `-` is a target, whatever it looks like. Validation happens before any work and stops the command at the first problem, in this order: an unknown option (`error: unknown option 'WORD'`); a `--max` without a decimal number after it (`error: bad --max value 'X'`, with `X` empty if the word is missing); no targets (`error: want needs at least one target`); the first target that is not a valid path without `%` (`error: bad path 'P'`).

Bringing a path up to date (*visiting* it) works like this. Each path is visited at most once per command; a second request for it gets the same outcome and prints nothing. The outcome is one of *source*, *fresh*, *built*, *failed*, *blocked*.

1. Find the rule for the path. If there is none: when the file exists the outcome is *source* (nothing is printed); otherwise print `error: no rule to make 'PATH'`, followed by ` (needed by 'REQUESTER')` when the path was visited as a dependency of another path, and the outcome is *failed*.
2. If the path is already being visited further up (a cycle), print `error: cycle A -> B -> ... -> A` where the list starts at the first occurrence of the path on the chain of paths being visited and ends with the path again. The outcome is *failed*.
3. Visit the dependencies (stems filled in) from left to right, so everything a path needs is reported before the path itself. If any dependency is *failed* or *blocked*, print `blocked PATH`; the outcome is *blocked*.
4. Decide whether the path is **stale**. It is stale if its file does not exist, or if any dependency has a stamp greater than the stamp of its file; an always-rule is always stale. Texts and digests play no role: a dependency that was rebuilt (or touched) makes everything above it stale even when its text came out identical, because every write ticks the clock. There is no early cutoff.
5. If the path is not stale, print `skip PATH`; the outcome is *fresh*.
6. Otherwise the action has to run. If the command has a budget (`--max N`) and `N` actions have already been executed by this command, print `halt: budget of N actions reached` and *stop the whole command* (nothing else is visited). `--max 0` therefore halts at the first action that has to run.
7. Run the action (this counts against the budget even if it fails; it also counts in `stats`). If it fails, print `fail PATH: MESSAGE`; the outcome is *failed*, and the file (if any) is left as it was.
8. If it succeeds, the file gets the new text and a new stamp (one tick) and the line is `same PATH` if the file already existed with exactly this text, else `run PATH`. The outcome is *built*.

Failure policy. Without `--keep-going` the command stops at the first failure (any line `fail ...`, `error: no rule ...` or `error: cycle ...` of this command): after that line nothing more is visited or printed except the final summary line. With `--keep-going` the command carries on: the other dependencies and the other targets are still visited, and only the paths that depend on a failure are *blocked*.

At the end of every `want` command that got past validation (also when it stopped early) it prints `tally: ran=R same=S skipped=K failed=F blocked=B`: the number of paths with the lines `run`, `same`, `skip`, `fail`/`error: no rule`/`error: cycle` (each such line counts one *failed*, also the one that stopped the command) and `blocked`. Sources and halting add nothing.

## 7. Status

`status TARGET...` (validation as for building; no targets: `error: status needs at least one target`) reports what a build would find, without running anything and without changing any file. It visits paths like a build does (once each, dependencies first, left to right; sources print nothing; `error: no rule to make ...` and `error: cycle ...` are printed in the same way), and prints for every derived path one line, in visiting order:

* nothing at all if one of its dependencies had an error (the path itself then counts as erroneous too);
* otherwise `stale PATH (REASON)` with the first applicable reason: `missing` (no file), `dep D` (`D` is the first dependency, left to right, that was reported stale), `always` (always-rule), `changed` (some dependency has a greater stamp);
* otherwise `fresh PATH`.

Note that a stale dependency makes every path above it stale in the report.

solution.src/hashing.py:
"""Content digests: FNV-1a (32 bit) over the UTF-8 bytes, shown as eight lower-case hex digits."""


def digest(text: str) -> str:
    h = 0x811C9DC5
    for b in text.encode("utf-8"):
        h ^= b
        h = (h * 0x01000193) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return "%08x" % h

start.README.md:
# weft: an incremental build engine for text artifacts

`weft` keeps a small in-memory store of text files, a set of build rules that derive some files from others, and it rebuilds only what is out of date. It is driven by a script on standard input and reports every step on standard output, so that its behaviour can be checked exactly. Nothing is read from or written to the real file system.

Build and run it as `python3 src/weft.py` (entry point `src/weft.py`; other modules go next to it in `src/`). The program reads the whole of standard input, runs the script line by line and exits.

## 1. Script and output

* A script is a sequence of lines. Leading and trailing white space of a line is ignored; empty lines and lines starting with `#` do nothing.
* The first word of a line is the command; words are separated by single or multiple spaces. Command names are lower-case and case-sensitive.
* Every command prints zero or more lines to standard output (given below). A failing command prints one `error: ...` line and the script continues with the next line.
* Exit status: `1` if at least one line starting with `error:` or `fail ` was printed during the run, otherwise `0`. Nothing is ever printed to standard error that matters.
* The commands are: `write`, `rule`, `build`, `show`, `digest`, `ls`, `stats`, `clean`, `touch`. Any other first word prints `error: unknown command 'WORD'`.

## 2. Paths, files and text

A path is made of letters, digits and the characters `_ . / -`. It is split at `/` into segments and no segment may be empty, `.` or `..` (so a path does not start or end with `/` and has no `//`). In rule targets and rule dependencies a path may also contain one `%` (see section 4). Anything else is a bad path: `error: bad path 'PATH'`.

The store maps paths to *files*. A file is a text (a string of ASCII characters; it may contain newlines and tabs) plus bookkeeping described below. A file is either a **source** (created by `write`) or **derived** (produced by a rule). A path is *derived* if a rule matches it (section 4), whether or not the file exists yet; every other path is a source path.

The *digest* of a text is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its UTF-8 bytes, written as eight lower-case hex digits: start with `h = 0x811c9dc5`; for each byte `b`, `h = h XOR b`, then `h = (h * 0x01000193) mod 2^32`. The digest of the empty text is `811c9dc5`.

The store has a **logical clock**, an integer that starts at 0. It is advanced by one (a *tick*) every time a file is written by `write` or by an action, and by `touch`; each file remembers the clock value of its last write as its *stamp*.

## 3. Commands that change or inspect files

* `write PATH [TEXT]` creates or replaces a source file. `TEXT` is everything after the single space that follows `PATH` (it may contain further spaces; white space at the end of the line is not part of it; it may be absent, giving an empty text). In `TEXT`, the escapes `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab) and `\\` (one backslash) are decoded; a backslash followed by any other character stays as it is. The file gets a new stamp (one tick). Prints `wrote PATH (N bytes)` where `N` is the length of the decoded text in bytes. Errors: no path -> `error: usage: write PATH [TEXT]`; a bad path; a derived path -> `error: 'PATH' is derived, not a source file`.
* `show PATH` prints `PATH = "TEXT"` with the text encoded the opposite way (a backslash becomes `\\`, a newline `\n`, a tab `\t`). Unknown file: `error: no such file 'PATH'`. Wrong word count: `error: usage: show PATH`.
* `digest PATH` prints `PATH DIGEST`. Same errors as `show` (usage text `usage: digest PATH`).
* `ls` prints one line `PATH DIGEST KIND` for every file in the store, sorted by path (plain byte order), where `KIND` is `derived` if the path is derived, else `source`. Arguments are ignored.
* `stats` prints `files=F rules=R actions=A clock=C`: the number of files, the number of rules, the number of action executions so far (failed attempts included; skipped ones not) and the clock. Arguments are ignored.
* `touch PATH` gives an existing file a new stamp (one tick) without changing its text and prints `touched PATH`. Errors: `error: usage: touch PATH`, `error: no such file 'PATH'`.
* `clean [PATH...]` deletes derived files. Without arguments it deletes every existing derived file; with arguments it deletes exactly those files. If an argument is not the path of an existing derived file the command prints `error: 'PATH' is not a derived file` for the first such argument (in the order given) and deletes nothing. Prints `cleaned N files` (`N` counts distinct deleted files; also for `0` and `1`). Deleting a file also forgets how it was built.

## 4. Rules

`rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` declares how `TARGET` is made. `<-` and `:` are words of their own. There may be no dependencies. A rule written with `:!` instead of `:` is an **always-rule** (see section 6). Arguments are the words after the action name.

Checks, in this order, each with its error (`error: ` is implied):

1. `rule syntax: rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` if the second word is not `<-`, there is no separator word, or no action name follows it.
2. `bad path 'P'` for the first of target, dependencies (left to right) that is not a valid path.
3. `stem in dependency without stem in target` if a dependency contains `%` but the target does not.
4. `unknown action 'NAME'`, or `bad arguments for 'NAME'` (section 5).
5. `duplicate rule for 'TARGET'` if an earlier rule has exactly the same target text.
6. `'FILE' already exists as a source file` if a file already in the store would be made by the new rule (for a pattern rule: the first such file in byte order); rules never take over existing files.

On success it prints `rule TARGET`.

**Pattern rules.** A target with a `%` is a pattern. `%` stands for a non-empty *stem* (it may contain `/`): the pattern `out/%.up` matches `out/a/b.up` with stem `a/b`, but not `out/.up`. In the dependencies of a pattern rule every `%` is replaced by the stem. Several dependencies may each contain a `%`; dependencies without one are fixed.

**Which rule makes a path.** An exact rule (target without `%`) whose target equals the path wins. Otherwise, among the pattern rules that match the path, the one with the most literal characters (target length minus one) wins; on a tie the earlier declared rule wins. If no rule matches, the path is a source path.

## 5. Actions

Every action computes the text of the target from the texts of the dependencies, taken in the order written. Let `IN` be those texts joined with a single `\n` between them (`IN` is empty when there are no dependencies); *lines of X* means X split at `\n`, dropping one empty last piece (so the empty text has no lines and `a\n` has one). Actions work on ASCII only.

| action | result |
|---|---|
| `cat` | `IN`. |
| `upper` | `IN` with `a`-`z` turned into `A`-`Z`. |
| `count` | the length of `IN` in characters, in decimal. |
| `lines` | the number of lines of `IN`, in decimal. |
| `head N` | the first `N` lines of `IN` joined with `\n` (all of them if there are fewer). `N` is 1 to 9 decimal digits. |
| `uniq` | the lines of `IN` with each run of identical consecutive lines reduced to one, joined with `\n`. |
| `grep WORD` | the lines of `IN` that contain `WORD` as a substring, joined with `\n` (exactly one argument). |
| `sum` | the sum of all white-space separated words of `IN` that look like an integer (an optional `-` and 1 to 9 digits), in decimal; other words are ignored. |
| `cap N` | like `sum`, but at most `N` (1 to 9 decimal digits). |
| `const [TEXT...]` | the arguments joined with single spaces (empty if none); the dependencies are not looked at. |
| `failif WORD` | `IN`, unless `IN` contains `WORD` as a substring: then the action *fails* with the message `found WORD` (exactly one argument). |
| `fail` | nothing: the action always *fails* with the message `always fails`. |

These are the only actions of this build; any other name is an unknown action. An action with arguments of the wrong number or shape is `bad arguments`. Actions without arguments listed above take none.

## 6. Building

`build [OPTION...] TARGET...` brings the targets up to date, in the order given. There are no options: a first word that starts with `-` is `error: unknown option 'WORD'`. Every word after the first word that does not start with `-` is a target, whatever it looks like. Validation happens before any work and stops the command at the first problem, in this order: an unknown option (`error: unknown option 'WORD'`); no targets (`error: build needs at least one target`); the first target that is not a valid path without `%` (`error: bad path 'P'`).

Bringing a path up to date (*visiting* it) works like this. Each path is visited at most once per command; a second request for it gets the same outcome and prints nothing. The outcome is one of *source*, *fresh*, *built*, *failed*, *blocked*.

1. Find the rule for the path. If there is none: when the file exists the outcome is *source* (nothing is printed); otherwise print `error: no rule to make 'PATH'`, followed by ` (needed by 'REQUESTER')` when the path was visited as a dependency of another path, and the outcome is *failed*.
2. If the path is already being visited further up (a cycle), print `error: cycle A -> B -> ... -> A` where the list starts at the first occurrence of the path on the chain of paths being visited and ends with the path again. The outcome is *failed*.
3. Visit the dependencies (stems filled in) from left to right, so everything a path needs is reported before the path itself. If any dependency is *failed* or *blocked*, print `blocked PATH`; the outcome is *blocked*.
4. Decide whether the path is **stale**. The *key* of a rule application is the digest of the text `ACTION` + `\x1f` (the byte 0x1f) + the digests of the dependency texts joined with `,`, where `ACTION` is the action name and its arguments joined with single spaces. Every derived file remembers the key of the application that made it. The path is stale if its file does not exist, or its remembered key differs from the current key (because a dependency's text changed, so that its digest changed); an always-rule is always stale. This gives **early cutoff**: when a dependency is rebuilt to exactly the same text, nothing that depends on it is rebuilt. Stamps play no role in this build.
5. If the path is not stale, print `skip PATH`; the outcome is *fresh*.
6. Otherwise run the action (it counts in `stats` even if it fails). If it fails, print `fail PATH: MESSAGE`; the outcome is *failed*, and the file (if any) is left as it was.
7. If it succeeds, the file gets the new text and a new stamp (one tick) and the new key and the line is `same PATH` if the file already existed with exactly this text, else `run PATH`. The outcome is *built*.

Failure policy. The command stops at the first failure (any line `fail ...`, `error: no rule ...` or `error: cycle ...` of this command): after that line nothing more is visited or printed except the final summary line.

At the end of every `build` command that got past validation (also when it stopped early) it prints `totals: ran=R same=S skipped=K failed=F blocked=B`: the number of paths with the lines `run`, `same`, `skip`, `fail`/`error: no rule`/`error: cycle` (each such line counts one *failed*, also the one that stopped the command) and `blocked`. Sources and halting add nothing.

## Examples

`weft` reading this on standard input:


# smelt: an incremental build engine for text artifacts

`smelt` keeps a small in-memory store of text files, a set of build rules that derive some files from others, and it rebuilds only what is out of date. It is driven by a script on standard input and reports every step on standard output, so that its behaviour can be checked exactly. Nothing is read from or written to the real file system.

Build and run it as `build/smelt`, built with `go build -o build/smelt .` (package `main` in the module root; `go.mod` is provided, standard library only). The program reads the whole of standard input, runs the script line by line and exits.

## 1. Script and output

* A script is a sequence of lines. Leading and trailing white space of a line is ignored; empty lines and lines starting with `#` do nothing.
* The first word of a line is the command; words are separated by single or multiple spaces. Command names are lower-case and case-sensitive.
* Every command prints zero or more lines to standard output (given below). A failing command prints one `error: ...` line and the script continues with the next line.
* Exit status: `1` if at least one line starting with `error:` or `fail ` was printed during the run, otherwise `0`. Nothing is ever printed to standard error that matters.
* The commands are: `put`, `rule`, `make`, `show`, `digest`, `ls`, `stats`, `status`, `clean`, `touch`. Any other first word prints `error: unknown command 'WORD'`.

## 2. Paths, files and text

A path is made of letters, digits and the characters `_ . / -`. It is split at `/` into segments and no segment may be empty, `.` or `..` (so a path does not start or end with `/` and has no `//`). In rule targets and rule dependencies a path may also contain one `%` (see section 4). Anything else is a bad path: `error: bad path 'PATH'`.

The store maps paths to *files*. A file is a text (a string of ASCII characters; it may contain newlines and tabs) plus bookkeeping described below. A file is either a **source** (created by `put`) or **derived** (produced by a rule). A path is *derived* if a rule matches it (section 4), whether or not the file exists yet; every other path is a source path.

The *digest* of a text is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its UTF-8 bytes, written as eight lower-case hex digits: start with `h = 0x811c9dc5`; for each byte `b`, `h = h XOR b`, then `h = (h * 0x01000193) mod 2^32`. The digest of the empty text is `811c9dc5`.

The store has a **logical clock**, an integer that starts at 0. It is advanced by one (a *tick*) every time a file is written by `put` or by an action, and by `touch`; each file remembers the clock value of its last write as its *stamp*.

## 3. Commands that change or inspect files

* `put PATH [TEXT]` creates or replaces a source file. `TEXT` is everything after the single space that follows `PATH` (it may contain further spaces; white space at the end of the line is not part of it; it may be absent, giving an empty text). In `TEXT`, the escapes `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab) and `\\` (one backslash) are decoded; a backslash followed by any other character stays as it is. The file gets a new stamp (one tick). Prints `wrote PATH (N bytes)` where `N` is the length of the decoded text in bytes. Errors: no path -> `error: usage: put PATH [TEXT]`; a bad path; a derived path -> `error: 'PATH' is derived, not a source file`.
* `show PATH` prints `PATH = "TEXT"` with the text encoded the opposite way (a backslash becomes `\\`, a newline `\n`, a tab `\t`). Unknown file: `error: no such file 'PATH'`. Wrong word count: `error: usage: show PATH`.
* `digest PATH` prints `PATH DIGEST`. Same errors as `show` (usage text `usage: digest PATH`).
* `ls` prints one line `PATH DIGEST KIND` for every file in the store, sorted by path (plain byte order), where `KIND` is `derived` if the path is derived, else `source`. Arguments are ignored.
* `stats` prints `files=F rules=R actions=A clock=C`: the number of files, the number of rules, the number of action executions so far (failed attempts included; skipped ones not) and the clock. Arguments are ignored.
* `touch PATH` gives an existing file a new stamp (one tick) without changing its text and prints `touched PATH`. Errors: `error: usage: touch PATH`, `error: no such file 'PATH'`.
* `clean [PATH...]` deletes derived files. Without arguments it deletes every existing derived file; with arguments it deletes exactly those files. If an argument is not the path of an existing derived file the command prints `error: 'PATH' is not a derived file` for the first such argument (in the order given) and deletes nothing. Prints `cleaned N files` (`N` counts distinct deleted files; also for `0` and `1`). Deleting a file also forgets how it was built.

## 4. Rules

`rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` declares how `TARGET` is made. `<-` and `:` are words of their own. There may be no dependencies. A rule written with `:!` instead of `:` is an **always-rule** (see section 6). Arguments are the words after the action name.

Checks, in this order, each with its error (`error: ` is implied):

1. `rule syntax: rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` if the second word is not `<-`, there is no separator word, or no action name follows it.
2. `bad path 'P'` for the first of target, dependencies (left to right) that is not a valid path.
3. `stem in dependency without stem in target` if a dependency contains `%` but the target does not.
4. `unknown action 'NAME'`, or `bad arguments for 'NAME'` (section 5).
5. `duplicate rule for 'TARGET'` if an earlier rule has exactly the same target text.
6. `'FILE' already exists as a source file` if a file already in the store would be made by the new rule (for a pattern rule: the first such file in byte order); rules never take over existing files.

On success it prints `rule TARGET`.

**Pattern rules.** A target with a `%` is a pattern. `%` stands for a non-empty *stem* (it may contain `/`): the pattern `out/%.up` matches `out/a/b.up` with stem `a/b`, but not `out/.up`. In the dependencies of a pattern rule every `%` is replaced by the stem. Several dependencies may each contain a `%`; dependencies without one are fixed.

**Which rule makes a path.** An exact rule (target without `%`) whose target equals the path wins. Otherwise, among the pattern rules that match the path, the one with the most literal characters (target length minus one) wins; on a tie the earlier declared rule wins. If no rule matches, the path is a source path.

## 5. Actions

Every action computes the text of the target from the texts of the dependencies, taken in the order written. Let `IN` be those texts joined with a single `\n` between them (`IN` is empty when there are no dependencies); *lines of X* means X split at `\n`, dropping one empty last piece (so the empty text has no lines and `a\n` has one). Actions work on ASCII only.

| action | result |
|---|---|
| `cat` | `IN`. |
| `lower` | `IN` with `A`-`Z` turned into `a`-`z`. |
| `rev` | `IN` with its characters in reverse order. |
| `count` | the length of `IN` in characters, in decimal. |
| `lines` | the number of lines of `IN`, in decimal. |
| `sort` | the lines of `IN` in byte order, joined with `\n`. |
| `grep WORD` | the lines of `IN` that contain `WORD` as a substring, joined with `\n` (exactly one argument). |
| `sum` | the sum of all white-space separated words of `IN` that look like an integer (an optional `-` and 1 to 9 digits), in decimal; other words are ignored. |
| `cap N` | like `sum`, but at most `N` (1 to 9 decimal digits). |
| `const [TEXT...]` | the arguments joined with single spaces (empty if none); the dependencies are not looked at. |
| `failif WORD` | `IN`, unless `IN` contains `WORD` as a substring: then the action *fails* with the message `found WORD` (exactly one argument). |
| `fail` | nothing: the action always *fails* with the message `always fails`. |

These are the only actions of this build; any other name is an unknown action. An action with arguments of the wrong number or shape is `bad arguments`. Actions without arguments listed above take none.

## 6. Building

`make [OPTION...] TARGET...` brings the targets up to date, in the order given. Options come first (words that start with `-` before the first target): `--keep-going` (or `-k`) and `--max N`. Every word after the first word that does not start with `-` is a target, whatever it looks like. Validation happens before any work and stops the command at the first problem, in this order: an unknown option (`error: unknown option 'WORD'`); a `--max` without a decimal number after it (`error: bad --max value 'X'`, with `X` empty if the word is missing); no targets (`error: make needs at least one target`); the first target that is not a valid path without `%` (`error: bad path 'P'`).

Bringing a path up to date (*visiting* it) works like this. Each path is visited at most once per command; a second request for it gets the same outcome and prints nothing. The outcome is one of *source*, *fresh*, *built*, *failed*, *blocked*.

1. Find the rule for the path. If there is none: when the file exists the outcome is *source* (nothing is printed); otherwise print `error: no rule to make 'PATH'`, followed by ` (needed by 'REQUESTER')` when the path was visited as a dependency of another path, and the outcome is *failed*.
2. If the path is already being visited further up (a cycle), print `error: cycle A -> B -> ... -> A` where the list starts at the first occurrence of the path on the chain of paths being visited and ends with the path again. The outcome is *failed*.
3. Visit the dependencies (stems filled in) from left to right, so everything a path needs is reported before the path itself. If any dependency is *failed* or *blocked*, print `blocked PATH`; the outcome is *blocked*.
4. Decide whether the path is **stale**. The *key* of a rule application is the digest of the text `ACTION` + `\x1f` (the byte 0x1f) + the digests of the dependency texts joined with `,`, where `ACTION` is the action name and its arguments joined with single spaces. Every derived file remembers the key of the application that made it. The path is stale if its file does not exist, or its remembered key differs from the current key (because a dependency's text changed, so that its digest changed); an always-rule is always stale. This gives **early cutoff**: when a dependency is rebuilt to exactly the same text, nothing that depends on it is rebuilt. Stamps play no role in this build.
5. If the path is not stale, print `skip PATH`; the outcome is *fresh*.
6. Otherwise the action has to run. If the command has a budget (`--max N`) and `N` actions have already been executed by this command, print `halt: budget of N actions reached` and *stop the whole command* (nothing else is visited). `--max 0` therefore halts at the first action that has to run.
7. Run the action (this counts against the budget even if it fails; it also counts in `stats`). If it fails, print `fail PATH: MESSAGE`; the outcome is *failed*, and the file (if any) is left as it was.
8. If it succeeds, the file gets the new text and a new stamp (one tick) and the new key and the line is `same PATH` if the file already existed with exactly this text, else `run PATH`. The outcome is *built*.

Failure policy. Without `--keep-going` the command stops at the first failure (any line `fail ...`, `error: no rule ...` or `error: cycle ...` of this command): after that line nothing more is visited or printed except the final summary line. With `--keep-going` the command carries on: the other dependencies and the other targets are still visited, and only the paths that depend on a failure are *blocked*.

At the end of every `make` command that got past validation (also when it stopped early) it prints `summary: ran=R same=S skipped=K failed=F blocked=B`: the number of paths with the lines `run`, `same`, `skip`, `fail`/`error: no rule`/`error: cycle` (each such line counts one *failed*, also the one that stopped the command) and `blocked`. Sources and halting add nothing.

## 7. Status

`status TARGET...` (validation as for building; no targets: `error: status needs at least one target`) reports what a build would find, without running anything and without changing any file. It visits paths like a build does (once each, dependencies first, left to right; sources print nothing; `error: no rule to make ...` and `error: cycle ...` are printed in the same way), and prints for every derived path one line, in visiting order:

* nothing at all if one of its dependencies had an error (the path itself then counts as erroneous too);
* otherwise `stale PATH (REASON)` with the first applicable reason: `missing` (no file), `dep D` (`D` is the first dependency, left to right, that was reported stale), `always` (always-rule), `changed` (the remembered key differs from the key computed from the current texts of the dependencies);
* otherwise `fresh PATH`.

Note that `status` is conservative: a path below a stale path is reported stale even though a build might cut off at the stale path.

# rivet: an incremental build engine for text artifacts

`rivet` keeps a small in-memory store of text files, a set of build rules that derive some files from others, and it rebuilds only what is out of date. It is driven by a script on standard input and reports every step on standard output, so that its behaviour can be checked exactly. Nothing is read from or written to the real file system.

Build and run it as `build/rivet`, built with `go build -o build/rivet .` (package `main` in the module root; `go.mod` is provided, standard library only). The program reads the whole of standard input, runs the script line by line and exits.

## 1. Script and output

* A script is a sequence of lines. Leading and trailing white space of a line is ignored; empty lines and lines starting with `#` do nothing.
* The first word of a line is the command; words are separated by single or multiple spaces. Command names are lower-case and case-sensitive.
* Every command prints zero or more lines to standard output (given below). A failing command prints one `error: ...` line and the script continues with the next line.
* Exit status: `1` if at least one line starting with `error:` or `fail ` was printed during the run, otherwise `0`. Nothing is ever printed to standard error that matters.
* The commands are: `write`, `rule`, `want`, `show`, `digest`, `ls`, `stats`, `touch`. Any other first word prints `error: unknown command 'WORD'`.

## 2. Paths, files and text

A path is made of letters, digits and the characters `_ . / -`. It is split at `/` into segments and no segment may be empty, `.` or `..` (so a path does not start or end with `/` and has no `//`). A `%` is not allowed in any path. Anything else is a bad path: `error: bad path 'PATH'`.

The store maps paths to *files*. A file is a text (a string of ASCII characters; it may contain newlines and tabs) plus bookkeeping described below. A file is either a **source** (created by `write`) or **derived** (produced by a rule). A path is *derived* if a rule matches it (section 4), whether or not the file exists yet; every other path is a source path.

The *digest* of a text is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its UTF-8 bytes, written as eight lower-case hex digits: start with `h = 0x811c9dc5`; for each byte `b`, `h = h XOR b`, then `h = (h * 0x01000193) mod 2^32`. The digest of the empty text is `811c9dc5`.

The store has a **logical clock**, an integer that starts at 0. It is advanced by one (a *tick*) every time a file is written by `write` or by an action, and by `touch`; each file remembers the clock value of its last write as its *stamp*.

## 3. Commands that change or inspect files

* `write PATH [TEXT]` creates or replaces a source file. `TEXT` is everything after the single space that follows `PATH` (it may contain further spaces; white space at the end of the line is not part of it; it may be absent, giving an empty text). In `TEXT`, the escapes `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab) and `\\` (one backslash) are decoded; a backslash followed by any other character stays as it is. The file gets a new stamp (one tick). Prints `wrote PATH (N bytes)` where `N` is the length of the decoded text in bytes. Errors: no path -> `error: usage: write PATH [TEXT]`; a bad path; a derived path -> `error: 'PATH' is derived, not a source file`.
* `show PATH` prints `PATH = "TEXT"` with the text encoded the opposite way (a backslash becomes `\\`, a newline `\n`, a tab `\t`). Unknown file: `error: no such file 'PATH'`. Wrong word count: `error: usage: show PATH`.
* `digest PATH` prints `PATH DIGEST`. Same errors as `show` (usage text `usage: digest PATH`).
* `ls` prints one line `PATH DIGEST KIND` for every file in the store, sorted by path (plain byte order), where `KIND` is `derived` if the path is derived, else `source`. Arguments are ignored.
* `stats` prints `files=F rules=R actions=A clock=C`: the number of files, the number of rules, the number of action executions so far (failed attempts included; skipped ones not) and the clock. Arguments are ignored.
* `touch PATH` gives an existing file a new stamp (one tick) without changing its text and prints `touched PATH`. Errors: `error: usage: touch PATH`, `error: no such file 'PATH'`.

## 4. Rules

`rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` declares how `TARGET` is made. `<-` and `:` are words of their own. There may be no dependencies. A rule written with `:!` instead of `:` is an **always-rule** (see section 6). Arguments are the words after the action name.

Checks, in this order, each with its error (`error: ` is implied):

1. `rule syntax: rule TARGET <- DEP... : ACTION [ARG...]` if the second word is not `<-`, there is no separator word, or no action name follows it.
2. `bad path 'P'` for the first of target, dependencies (left to right) that is not a valid path.
4. `unknown action 'NAME'`, or `bad arguments for 'NAME'` (section 5).
5. `duplicate rule for 'TARGET'` if an earlier rule has exactly the same target text.
6. `'FILE' already exists as a source file` if a file already in the store would be made by the new rule (for a pattern rule: the first such file in byte order); rules never take over existing files.

On success it prints `rule TARGET`.

**Which rule makes a path.** An exact rule (target without `%`) whose target equals the path wins. If no rule matches, the path is a source path.

## 5. Actions

Every action computes the text of the target from the texts of the dependencies, taken in the order written. Let `IN` be those texts joined with a single `\n` between them (`IN` is empty when there are no dependencies); *lines of X* means X split at `\n`, dropping one empty last piece (so the empty text has no lines and `a\n` has one). Actions work on ASCII only.

| action | result |
|---|---|
| `cat` | `IN`. |
| `upper` | `IN` with `a`-`z` turned into `A`-`Z`. |
| `rev` | `IN` with its characters in reverse order. |
| `count` | the length of `IN` in characters, in decimal. |
| `head N` | the first `N` lines of `IN` joined with `\n` (all of them if there are fewer). `N` is 1 to 9 decimal digits. |
| `uniq` | the lines of `IN` with each run of identical consecutive lines reduced to one, joined with `\n`. |
| `grep WORD` | the lines of `IN` that contain `WORD` as a substring, joined with `\n` (exactly one argument). |
| `tag NAME` | `<NAME>` followed by `IN` followed by `</NAME>`; `NAME` is one argument: a letter followed by letters and digits. |
| `sum` | the sum of all white-space separated words of `IN` that look like an integer (an optional `-` and 1 to 9 digits), in decimal; other words are ignored. |
| `const [TEXT...]` | the arguments joined with single spaces (empty if none); the dependencies are not looked at. |
| `fail` | nothing: the action always *fails* with the message `always fails`. |

These are the only actions of this build; any other name is an unknown action. An action with arguments of the wrong number or shape is `bad arguments`. Actions without arguments listed above take none.

## 6. Building

`want [OPTION...] TARGET...` brings the targets up to date, in the order given. Options come first (words that start with `-` before the first target): `--keep-going` (or `-k`). Every word after the first word that does not start with `-` is a target, whatever it looks like. Validation happens before any work and stops the command at the first problem, in this order: an unknown option (`error: unknown option 'WORD'`); no targets (`error: want needs at least one target`); the first target that is not a valid path without `%` (`error: bad path 'P'`).

Bringing a path up to date (*visiting* it) works like this. Each path is visited at most once per command; a second request for it gets the same outcome and prints nothing. The outcome is one of *source*, *fresh*, *built*, *failed*, *blocked*.

1. Find the rule for the path. If there is none: when the file exists the outcome is *source* (nothing is printed); otherwise print `error: no rule to make 'PATH'`, followed by ` (needed by 'REQUESTER')` when the path was visited as a dependency of another path, and the outcome is *failed*.
2. If the path is already being visited further up (a cycle), print `error: cycle A -> B -> ... -> A` where the list starts at the first occurrence of the path on the chain of paths being visited and ends with the path again. The outcome is *failed*.
3. Visit the dependencies (stems filled in) from left to right, so everything a path needs is reported before the path itself. If any dependency is *failed* or *blocked*, print `blocked PATH`; the outcome is *blocked*.
4. Decide whether the path is **stale**. It is stale if its file does not exist, or if any dependency has a stamp greater than the stamp of its file; an always-rule is always stale. Texts and digests play no role: a dependency that was rebuilt (or touched) makes everything above it stale even when its text came out identical, because every write ticks the clock. There is no early cutoff.
5. If the path is not stale, print `skip PATH`; the outcome is *fresh*.
6. Otherwise run the action (it counts in `stats` even if it fails). If it fails, print `fail PATH: MESSAGE`; the outcome is *failed*, and the file (if any) is left as it was.
7. If it succeeds, the file gets the new text and a new stamp (one tick) and the line is `same PATH` if the file already existed with exactly this text, else `run PATH`. The outcome is *built*.

Failure policy. Without `--keep-going` the command stops at the first failure (any line `fail ...`, `error: no rule ...` or `error: cycle ...` of this command): after that line nothing more is visited or printed except the final summary line. With `--keep-going` the command carries on: the other dependencies and the other targets are still visited, and only the paths that depend on a failure are *blocked*.

At the end of every `want` command that got past validation (also when it stopped early) it prints `tally: ran=R same=S skipped=K failed=F blocked=B`: the number of paths with the lines `run`, `same`, `skip`, `fail`/`error: no rule`/`error: cycle` (each such line counts one *failed*, also the one that stopped the command) and `blocked`. Sources and halting add nothing.
